title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
subtitle: Learn what really changed from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, so you can pick settings for clients, load balancers and timeouts with care.

c.v: A shopping app loads its home screen with about forty small API calls. The API runs on HTTP/1.1. On slow networks, the screen takes many seconds to fill, because requests wait in line for free connections.
The team turns on HTTP/2 at the
load balancer
. Now all forty calls share one connection. On office Wi-Fi, the home screen is much faster, and everyone is happy.
Then support tickets arrive from users on trains. Sometimes the whole screen freezes for a second or two, and then everything appears at once. The team checks the servers, and they answered fast.
The cause was one lost
packet
. HTTP/2 sends every request over one
TCP
connection. TCP hands data to the app only in order. So one lost packet stalls every request on that connection, even requests the loss did not touch
. The fix was to also offer HTTP/3 for clients that can use it.
This story is made up. But the behaviour is real and written in the standards.
HTTP has two parts:
Semantics
: what a message means. Methods like GET and POST, status codes like 404, and headers.
RFC
9110 says all three major HTTP versions rely on the same semantics
Wire format
: how those messages travel. This is the part each version changes.
So your handler code does not change when the version changes. What changes is speed, how many connections you hold, and what happens when packets are lost.
HTTP/1.1
sends text messages over TCP. It cannot mix requests on one connection, so clients open several connections to work in parallel
HTTP/2
uses binary frames instead of text, over one TCP connection. Many requests run at the same time, each in its own stream
HTTP/3
keeps the idea of streams, but runs on
QUIC
, over
UDP
. A lost packet blocks only the streams it carried
The key idea.
Each new HTTP version keeps the same meaning and fixes the waiting of the version before. HTTP/2 removes waiting between requests. HTTP/3 removes waiting caused by TCP itself.
Step through three requests, A, B and C, with one lost packet. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
HTTP/1.1: one request at a time
HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default. One connection can serve many requests, one after another
. This is
keep-alive
, and it saves a new
TCP handshake
for each request.
Pipelining lets a client send several requests without waiting. But the server must send the responses in the same order
. So one slow response still blocks the rest
. In practice, clients open several connections to one server instead
. RFC 9112 asks clients to limit how many they open, because each one uses server resources. It gives no fixed maximum
Many connections also make
congestion control
work less well, because TCP does not share it across connections
HTTP/2: many streams, one TCP connection
HTTP/2 cuts each message into binary
frames
. Each request and response pair gets its own
stream
, and frames from many streams mix on one connection
. This is called
multiplexing
. RFC 9113 says clients should not open more than one HTTP/2 connection to a given host and port
Each side tells the other how many streams it may open at once. RFC 9113 recommends at least 100, so that parallel work is not limited
HPACK
Requests to one server repeat the same headers again and again, which wastes
bandwidth
. Before HPACK, SPDY compressed headers with DEFLATE. The CRIME attack showed that this could leak secrets
. HPACK instead keeps tables of headers that both sides already know. A header can then be sent as a small index
Server push.
HTTP/2 added an optional way for a server to send responses the client did not ask for yet
. It did not work out well. RFC 9113 itself says push is hard to use well, because the server must guess what the client will ask for
. Only 1.25% of HTTP/2 sites used it. Studies had mixed results, with no clear overall gain and often worse performance
. Chrome announced that it would turn push off by default in version 106. The post suggests
103 Early Hints
and preload instead
What HTTP/2 did not fix.
TCP still sees one ordered stream of bytes. RFC 9113 says plainly that TCP
head-of-line blocking
is not addressed
. A lost packet stalls every stream, even streams the loss did not touch
. See
TCP/IP and the network stack
for why TCP works this way.
HTTP/3: streams that do not block each other
HTTP/3 maps each request and response to its own
QUIC
stream. If one stream is blocked or loses a packet, other streams still make progress
. QUIC does not keep any order between bytes on different streams
Two other changes matter:
Faster setup.
QUIC includes
TLS
1.3. RFC 9114 says this gives security like TLS over TCP, with faster connection setup
. See
TLS and secure connections
for the handshake.
Connection migration
A QUIC connection has connection IDs, not only an address and port. These IDs let a connection survive a change of address
. Only the client can start a migration, and only after the handshake is confirmed
HPACK assumes data arrives in order, which QUIC does not promise across streams. So HTTP/3 uses a new format, QPACK
How a client picks a version
ALPN
In the TLS handshake, the client sends a list of protocols it supports. The server picks one. This adds no extra round trips
. HTTP/2 over TLS uses the name
h2
, and HTTP/3 uses
h3
Alt-Svc
The URL is still
https://
, so the client needs a sign that the server also speaks HTTP/3. The server can send one in a response header, like
. The
ma
value is how many seconds the client may remember this. Without it, the default is 24 hours
. The URL and origin do not change
Alt-Svc is only a hint. The client may try QUIC after it sees one
. If UDP is blocked, RFC 9114 tells clients to use HTTP over TCP instead
. So keep TCP serving too.
What changes for backend engineers
Load balancers often split the versions.
An AWS Application Load Balancer can accept HTTP/2 from browsers. By default it still sends requests to your servers over HTTP/1.1
. You can choose HTTP/2 or
gRPC
per target group, only behind an HTTPS listener. With HTTP/2 chosen, requests that arrive as HTTP/1.1 fail
One connection means less spread.
An HTTP/2 client should open only one connection per host and port
. Behind a
layer 4
balancer, all its requests then reach one server. See
Load balancing
Closing gracefully.
HTTP/2 has a GOAWAY frame. Its last stream ID tells the client which requests the server may have acted on
. The rest were not processed, so they can be retried on a new connection
. In HTTP/1.1, a side that wants to time out should close the connection gracefully
Retries
Idempotent
requests can be retried automatically after a connection fails
. Others should not be, unless the client knows the first try was not applied
. See
Idempotency, retries and timeouts
HTTP/1.1
One at a time. Clients open several.
Only that connection.
Simple service calls, old clients, debugging by hand.
HTTP/2
Many streams on one TCP connection.
All streams on the connection.
Browsers and APIs with many small requests, gRPC.
HTTP/3
Many streams on one QUIC connection.
Only streams with data in that packet.
Users on phones and lossy networks.
Server push
Extra responses the client did not ask for.
Not relevant.
Avoid. Chrome turned it off by default. Use
103 Early Hints
or preload.
Simple rule:
for users on the internet, serve HTTP/2, and add HTTP/3 at the edge if your
CDN
or load balancer supports it. Inside your data center, the version matters less than reusing connections.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: When someone says "HTTP/2 will make it faster", ask:
"Faster for which clients, on which network?"
Measure before and after.
Know which version each hop speaks: client to CDN, CDN to load balancer, load balancer to server. They often differ.
Check stream limits on both sides. A low stream limit on one HTTP/2 connection makes extra requests wait in a queue.
During deploys, make sure servers send GOAWAY and drain, so clients move to a new connection without errors.
Retry only idempotent requests after a connection drops. Use an
idempotency key
for payments.
When you turn on HTTP/3, also watch QUIC errors and UDP traffic. Keep TCP working as the
fallback
"Here is our nginx config. Which HTTP versions does it serve to clients, and which does it use to our upstream servers? Show the exact lines."
"Our Go service calls another service over HTTP/2. Explain how the client reuses connections, and what happens to in-flight requests when the server sends GOAWAY."
"Write a load test that compares HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 with 2% packet loss. Explain what I should expect and why."
Every setting the agent names exists in your server or library version. Check the docs.
The agent does not suggest HTTP/2 server push. Chrome turned it off by default
Claims like "HTTP/3 is always faster" are tested on your own traffic, with loss and without.
Retries are added only for idempotent requests.
The agent knows that the load balancer may speak a different version to your servers than to clients.
TCP/IP and the network stack
: handshakes, packet loss and head-of-line blocking.
TLS and secure connections
: how ALPN fits into the handshake.
WebSockets, SSE and long polling
: long-lived connections on top of HTTP.
CDNs and HTTP caching
: where HTTP/3 is often turned on first.

q.v: You move an API from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2. What do your handlers need to change?

options.v: Every handler must read binary frames.
Nothing in the meaning. Methods, status codes and headers stay the same.
All GET requests must become POST.

why.v: RFC 9110 says all three major HTTP versions rely on the same semantics. Only how messages travel on the wire changes.

q.v: Ten requests share one HTTP/2 connection on a phone. One TCP packet is lost. What happens?

options.v: Only the request in that packet waits.
All requests behind the lost packet wait, because TCP gives bytes only in order.
HTTP/2 switches to UDP for that request.

why.v: TCP cannot see HTTP/2 streams, so a lost packet stalls them all. RFC 9113 says HTTP/2 does not fix TCP head-of-line blocking.

q.v: How does a browser first learn that your site also speaks HTTP/3?

options.v: From an Alt-Svc header in an earlier response, or another discovery method.
The browser always tries UDP first for every site.
From the URL, which must start with h3://.

why.v: RFC 9114 describes Alt-Svc as one way to advertise an HTTP/3 endpoint. The URL stays https://.

q.v: Your AWS Application Load Balancer accepts HTTP/2 from browsers. By default, what does it speak to your servers?

options.v: HTTP/1.1, unless you change the target group's protocol version.

why.v: AWS documents that the load balancer sends requests to targets with HTTP/1.1 by default.

sources.title: Thomson and Benfield (eds.), RFC 9113: HTTP/2 (IETF, 2022)
sources.note: Section 1 says why HTTP/2 exists. Frames, streams, SETTINGS, GOAWAY and connection rules follow.

sources.note: Section 1 explains why headers needed a new, safer compression format.

sources.note: Section 1 compares the three versions. Section 3.1 explains how a client finds an HTTP/3 server.
